tones.title: Mandarin Tones
tones.subtitle: The pitch that turns one syllable into four different words.

ps: Mandarin is a tonal language: the same syllable spoken at a different pitch is a completely different word. This is the single hardest thing for beginners and the most important thing to get right.
The classic example is ma. Spoken at four different pitches it means four totally unrelated things, so wrong tones can lead to funny or embarrassing mistakes.
list: First tone (mā 妈) — high and flat, like holding a steady note
Second tone (má 麻) — rises up, like a question 'eh?'
Third tone (mǎ 马) — dips down then rises, the low-dip tone
Fourth tone (mà 骂) — a sharp, quick fall, like a command

example.py: Mā ma qí mǎ
example.en: Mom rides a horse.

ps: Many short grammatical words and repeated characters are spoken with no fixed tone — light, short and unstressed. This is called the neutral tone (轻声).
The neutral tone is softer and shorter than a full tone. Missing it is a very common beginner tell.

sections.h: Tone Sandhi: 一 and 不
ps: A few words change their tone depending on what comes next. The two you need immediately are 一 (one) and 不 (not).
一 is originally first tone, but it becomes second tone before a fourth tone, and fourth tone before any other tone. 不 is originally fourth tone, but it becomes second tone before another fourth tone.
list: yí gè 一个 (one + 4th) → 一 reads second tone: 'one (thing)'
yì zhí 一直 (one + 2nd) → 一 reads fourth tone: 'always / straight'
bú shì 不是 (not + 4th) → 不 reads second tone: 'is not'
bù lái 不来 (not + 2nd) → 不 stays fourth tone: 'not coming'

example.py: bú shì yí gè
example.en: It is not one.

ps: When two third tones sit next to each other, the first one changes to sound like a second tone. This happens automatically and you don't choose it.
Between more than two third tones, native speakers apply the same rule naturally. You don't need to memorise every case yet — just be aware it exists.

pinyin.title: Pinyin
pinyin.subtitle: The romanisation that tells you how to pronounce anything.

ps: Every Mandarin syllable starts with an initial (a consonant) and ends with a final (a vowel or vowel+nucleus). The 21 initials are the consonants you start a word with.
Most initials sound like English, but watch zh/ch/sh/r (retroflex, curled tongue) and the difference between z/c/s and zh/ch/sh.
list: b p m f — bō pō mō fō
d t n l — dē tē nē lē
g k h — gē kē hē
j q x — jī qī xī
zh ch sh r — zhī chī shī rī
z c s — zī cī sī
y w — yī wū (act as 'empty' starters)

ps: Finals are the vowel part of a syllable. They come as single vowels, compound vowels, and nasal endings.
Single vowels are the most stable. Compound vowels glide from one vowel to another. Nasal finals end in -n or -ng.
list: Single finals: a o e i u ü — 'ah, or, uh, ee, oo, yu'
Compound finals: ai ei ao ou, ia ie iao iu, ua uo uai ui, üe
Nasal finals: an en in un ün, ang eng ing ong
Tip: ü is like saying 'ee' while rounding your lips.

sections.h: Spelling Rules: ü and the Empty Starters
ps: Pinyin follows a few fixed spelling shortcuts that look confusing at first but are very logical once you know them.
After j, q, x and y, the two dots on ü are dropped and it is written as u — but you still pronounce it as ü!
list: ü drops its dots after j/q/x/y: jǔ = ju (pronounced jü), xuě = xue (pronounced xüe)
Standing alone, i becomes yi, u becomes wu, ü becomes yu: yi, wu, yu
iou, uei, uen are shortened: liu (liú), gui (guì), lun (lún)
So 'ju' is never 'joo' — it is 'jü'.

example.py: Wǒ qù yīyuàn
example.en: I'm going to the hospital.

ps: The tone mark always sits on the main vowel of a syllable — the loudest, openest vowel.
When a syllable has i, the tone mark goes on the i and the dot disappears.
list: Mark on a/o/e, or on the loudest vowel: hǎo, máo, lèi
iu and ui: mark goes on the last vowel: liù, guì
Mark on i: the dot is removed — nǐ, lǐ, xī
Neutral tone gets no mark at all

initials.title: Initials · 声母
initials.subtitle: The 21 consonant starts that open almost every syllable.

ps: A Chinese syllable is split into an initial (声母 shēngmǔ, the opening consonant) and a final (韵母 yùnmǔ, the vowel ending). There are 21 initials, and most map closely to English sounds.
The tricky ones are the retroflex group (zh ch sh r), where the tongue curls up, and the breathy vs. voiced pairs (b/p, d/t, g/k).
list: b, p, m, f — like English b/p/m/f but p/f are more breathy
d, t, n, l — d/t are lighter than English; n/l confuse many learners
g, k, h — h is a soft throat sound like the 'ch' in Scottish loch
j, q, x — all said with a smile, tongue flat behind the lower teeth
zh, ch, sh, r — curl the tongue tip up; r is voiced and soft
z, c, s — tongue flat; c is like 'ts' in cats

ps: The fastest progress comes from contrasting sounds that English merges. Record yourself and compare the retroflex vs. flat pairs.

example.py: Wǒ zhǎo sì hào xiàn
example.en: I'm looking for Line 4.

finals.title: Finals · 韵母
finals.subtitle: The vowel endings — simple, compound and nasal.

ps: The six simple finals are a, o, e, i, u, ü. They combine into compound finals (ai, ei, ao, ou, ia, ie, uo, üe) and nasal finals ending in -n (an, en, in) or -ng (ang, eng, ing, ong).
The -n vs. -ng contrast matters a lot: 心 xīn (heart) vs. 星 xīng (star) differ only in that final nasal.
ü sounds like the 'ee' in see with rounded lips. After j, q, x, y the two dots are dropped in writing (ju, qu, xu, yu) but the sound is still ü.

example.py: Wǒ qù mǎi yú
example.en: I'm going to buy fish.

tone-marks.title: Marking the Tones · 声调标注
tone-marks.subtitle: Where the tone mark sits — and why it matters.

ps: Every syllable carries one tone mark over a vowel. When there are several vowels, the mark follows the priority a > o > e > i > u > ü. On i or u the dot is replaced (nǐ, hǎo).
When i and u stand together, the mark goes on the second one: 好 hǎo, 六 liù, 水 shuǐ.
list: mā (1st) má (2nd) mǎ (3rd) mà (4th) — the classic ma drill
ā á ǎ à · ō ó ǒ ò · ē é ě è — practice each vowel row
i/u pairs: liù (six), shuǐ (water), jiǔ (nine)

sections.h: Read the mark, not your habit
ps: English stress is loudness; Chinese tone is pitch shape. Saying a syllable with the wrong tone often changes the word entirely — 买 mǎi (buy) vs. 卖 mài (sell).

example.py: Wǒ yào mǎi, bú shì yào mài
example.en: I want to buy, not sell.

neutral-tone.title: The Neutral Tone · 轻声
neutral-tone.subtitle: Short, light syllables that carry no full tone.

ps: Some syllables lose their own tone and become short and light — the neutral tone (轻声 qīngshēng), written with no mark. It is common on the second character of family words, particles, and repeated verbs.
The neutral syllable is quicker and lower, never stressed.
的 de, 了 le, 吗 ma, 呢 ne are grammatical particles and are read light. Keeping them light instantly makes your Chinese sound more natural.

sandhi-yi.title: How 一 Changes Tone · 一的变调
sandhi-yi.subtitle: 一 is a tone chameleon.

ps: Alone or counting, 一 is yī (1st tone). Before a 4th-tone syllable it becomes yí (2nd tone); before 1st/2nd/3rd tones it becomes yì (4th tone).
This is purely spoken sandhi — pinyin in dictionaries often still prints yī, but native speakers shift automatically.
list: yī (alone): 一 二 三 = yī èr sān
yí + 4th: 一个 yíge, 一样 yíyàng, 一共 yígòng
yì + non-4th: 一天 yìtiān, 一年 yìnián, 一起 yìqǐ

ps: 一 appears constantly before measure words, so you meet the sandhi constantly: 一杯 yìbēi (a cup), but 一个 yíge (a piece).

sandhi-bu.title: How 不 Changes Tone · 不的变调
sandhi-bu.subtitle: 不 turns 2nd tone before a 4th tone.

ps: 不 is normally bù (4th tone). Before another 4th-tone syllable it becomes bú (2nd tone): 不是 búshì, 不要 búyào, 不客气 bú kèqi.
Between the two characters of a verb (A不A questions) it is often neutral: 好不好 hǎobuhǎo.
Keep bù before non-4th tones and bú before 4th tones.

example.py: Wǒ bú qù, tā yě bú qù
example.en: I'm not going, and he isn't either.

third-tone-sandhi.title: Third-Tone Changes · 三声变调
third-tone-sandhi.subtitle: Two third tones never stay two third tones.

ps: When two 3rd-tone syllables meet, the first becomes a 2nd tone. 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but pronounced ní hǎo. 可以 kěyǐ → kéyǐ.
Before any other tone, a 3rd tone is usually pronounced as a low 'half third' — a dip, no rise.
The full 3rd-tone rise-fall is mainly used when a word is said alone or emphasized. In normal speech, treat it mostly as a low tone to sound natural.

example.py: Wǒ hén hǎo (written wǒ hěn hǎo)
example.en: I'm fine.

retroflex.title: Retroflex Sounds · 翘舌音
retroflex.subtitle: Curl the tongue for zh, ch, sh, r.

ps: For zh, ch, sh, r, curl the tongue tip up toward (not touching) the roof of the mouth. For z, c, s the tongue stays flat behind the lower teeth. Many southern accents and learners merge these — keep them apart to be understood.
r is voiced and gentle, like the r in 'ray' but softer, never like an English rolled r.
Hold a mirror or a finger under the tongue: the tip should rise for the retroflex set.

tricky-vowels.title: Tricky Vowels · 易错韵母
tricky-vowels.subtitle: The sounds that trip English speakers.

ps: Chinese e is not the English 'e' in bed — it's a flat, mid 'uh' sound (饿 è = hungry). o is more like 'aw' in 'law' with rounded lips (我 wǒ). ü needs rounded lips on an 'ee' tongue (绿 lǜ).
The final -i after zh/ch/sh/r and z/c/s is a buzzed vowel, not a normal 'ee': 知 zhī, 吃 chī, 字 zì.
The -ian final sounds closer to 'yen': 天 tiān (sky/day), 钱 qián (money), 点 diǎn (point/o'clock). Don't stretch the a.

pinyin-spelling.title: Pinyin Spelling Rules · 拼写规则
pinyin-spelling.subtitle: Why some syllables look different from how they sound.

sections.h: j q x + ü drops the dots
ps: Because u never follows j, q, x in Chinese, writing ju/qu/xu unambiguously means jü/qü/xü — the dots are simply removed: 句 jù, 去 qù, 需 xū.
Syllables starting with i/u/ü get a leading y/w: i→yi, u→wu, ü→yu; ie→ye, uo→wo, üe→yue.
list: jū, jú, jǔ, jù = the syllable jü in four tones
yī, wǔ, yú = standalone i, u, ü
yè (night), wǒ (I), yuè (month) show the y/w lead-in

ps: When syllables could be misread, an apostrophe splits them: 西安 Xī'ān (the city) vs. 先 xiān; 皮袄 pí'ǎo (fur coat) vs. 漂 piǎo.

stress-rhythm.title: Rhythm & Stress · 轻重节奏
stress-rhythm.subtitle: Chinese beats by the syllable, not the word.

ps: Each Chinese character gets roughly even time — there is no strong-weak stress like English 'PHO-to'. Content syllables keep their full tone and length; grammatical particles (的, 了, 吗, 们) go short and neutral.
Clapping once per character as you speak builds good rhythm.
list: 我的书 wǒde shū — de is light, shū is full
朋友们 péngyoumen — both 友 and 们 can lighten
吃了吗 chīle ma — particles clipped quick

ps: Saying 北京 as 'bei-JING' with a heavy jump sounds foreign. Keep both syllables level: Běijīng.
Spend 5 minutes a day on minimal-pair listening: tones first, then finals (-n/-ng), then initials (s/sh, n/l, c/ch).
Use HanVerse scenes: tap a word, hear it, then say it before the audio repeats.
Some dialect backgrounds swap n and l (南 nán vs. 蓝 lán) or h and f (飞 fēi vs. 灰 huī). Drill these deliberately.

example.py: Húnán rén hē niúnǎi
example.en: A Hunan person drinks milk.

characters.title: Chinese Characters
characters.subtitle: How Han characters are built, one stroke and radical at a time.

ps: Almost every character fits into one of four layout patterns. Once you spot the pattern, the character stops looking like a random squiggle.
Left-right and top-bottom are by far the most common in everyday words.
list: Left-right (左右结构): 好 hǎo, 说 shuō, 你 nǐ
Top-bottom (上下结构): 字 zì, 家 jiā, 意 yì
Enclosing (包围结构): 国 guó, 回 huí, 问 wèn
Standalone (独体字): 人 rén, 山 shān, 水 shuǐ

ps: Every character is made from a small set of strokes. Learning the main five makes writing feel orderly and helps you look up characters.
Strokes are written in a conventional order: top before bottom, left before right, horizontal before vertical.
list: 横 héng (horizontal): 一
竖 shù (vertical): in 十
撇 piě (left-falling): in 人
点 diǎn (dot): in 主
折 zhé (turning/bend): in 口, 月

ps: Radicals are the clue-parts of a character. One side often hints at the meaning, the other hints at the sound.
Learning a handful of high-frequency radicals lets you guess the topic of a new character before you even know how to read it.
list: 氵 (water radical) — 河 hé river, 海 hǎi sea, 洗 xǐ wash
口 (mouth radical) — 吃 chī eat, 喝 hē drink, 叫 jiào call
木 (tree/wood radical) — 树 shù tree, 林 lín forest, 桌 zhuō table
亻 (person radical) — 你 nǐ you, 他 tā he, 住 zhù live
讠 (speech radical) — 说 shuō speak, 话 huà words, 请 qǐng please
女 (woman radical) — 好 hǎo good, 妈 mā mom, 她 tā she
心 / 忄 (heart radical) — 想 xiǎng think, 快 kuài fast, 怕 pà fear
火 / 灬 (fire radical) — 火 huǒ fire, 热 rè hot, 煮 zhǔ boil

ps: A few simple characters are repeated everywhere and are worth learning first. Many are ancient pictures of what they mean.
These characters also act as building blocks inside bigger characters.

strokes.title: Basic Strokes · 基本笔画
strokes.subtitle: Every character is built from eight core strokes.

ps: Chinese characters are written with a small set of strokes: horizontal 一 héng, vertical 丨 shù, dot 丶 diǎn, left-fall 丿 piě, right-fall ㇏ nà, rising ㇀ tí, hook 亅 gōu, and bend ㇈ zhé.
Each stroke is drawn in one confident motion; there is no sketching back and forth.
list: 一 (horizontal) left → right
丨 (vertical) top → bottom
丿 (left-fall) and ㇏ (right-fall) form 人 rén (person)
十 = one horizontal + one vertical

ps: 人 person, 大 big (person with legs spread), 天 sky (big + a top line) — you can see characters stacking strokes into meaning.

stroke-order.title: Stroke Order · 笔顺
stroke-order.subtitle: Rules that make characters fast and balanced.

ps: Follow these and characters look right: top before bottom (三), left before right (你), horizontal before vertical (十), outside before inside then close the box (国), middle before the two sides (小).
Correct order also predicts the character in handwriting recognition and dictionaries.
list: 十: horizontal first, then vertical
口: left-fall side, then top/right, then bottom seal
国: outer frame first, inner 玉, then the closing line
我: top-left down, ending with the long right-fall

ps: Following stroke order builds muscle memory so characters stick. Phone keyboards and apps also assume it when recognizing your handwriting.

example.py: Qǐng xiě yíxià nǐ de míngzi
example.en: Please write your name.

radicals.title: Radicals · 偏旁部首
radicals.subtitle: The semantic Lego of Chinese characters.

ps: A radical (部首 bùshǒu) is the component that often hints at meaning. 氵(water) appears in 河 river, 海 sea, 汤 soup; 讠(speech) in 说 say, 语 language, 请 please.
Radicals are also how Chinese dictionaries group and look up characters.
Most characters are 形声字: one part hints meaning (radical), the other hints sound. 清 qīng has water 氵 + 青 qīng; 情 qíng has heart 忄 + 青 qīng.

pictophonetic.title: Phono-Semantic Characters · 形声字
pictophonetic.subtitle: One part for meaning, one for sound.

ps: Roughly 80% of Chinese characters combine a semantic radical with a phonetic component. Spotting this turns 'random squiggles' into a reusable system.
The phonetic part gives a rhyme-like clue, not always an exact sound.
list: 妈 mā (mom): woman 女 + 马 mǎ (sound clue)
吗 ma (question): mouth 口 + 马 mǎ
园 yuán (garden): enclosure 囗 + 元 yuán
房 fáng (room): door 户 + 方 fāng

ps: Learn families together: 包 bāo gives 抱 bào (hug, hand), 饱 bǎo (full, food), 跑 pǎo (run, foot).
Components sit left-right (你 = 亻+尔), top-bottom (要 = 覀+女), inside-outside (国), or half-surround (这 = 辶+文). Recognizing layout helps you parse unfamiliar characters.
The radical usually occupies a fixed slot — 亻, 氵, 讠 on the left; 艹, ⺮, 心 on top or bottom.
Instead of rote strokes, name the parts: 休 = 亻(person) + 木(tree) = a person resting by a tree = 'to rest'.

common-radicals.title: High-Frequency Radicals · 常见部首
common-radicals.subtitle: Twenty radicals unlock hundreds of characters.

ps: Learn these meaning-radicals first: 亻person, 女 woman, 口 mouth, 手/扌 hand, 足/⻊ foot, 心/忄 heart, 目 eye, 日 sun/day, 月 moon/flesh, 木 tree, 氵 water, 火/灬 fire, 土 earth, 金/钅 metal.
Some radicals compress in a character: 水→氵, 火→灬, 人→亻, 心→忄, 犬→犭, 金→钅. Same meaning, tighter form.

counting-strokes.title: Counting Strokes · 数笔画
counting-strokes.subtitle: How dictionaries and forms sort characters.

ps: Chinese forms and dictionaries index characters by stroke count. 一 is 1 stroke, 人 is 2, 口 is 3, 日 is 4, 田 is 5. Count each stroke once, including hooks and dots.
A single connected motion is one stroke, even if it bends (㇈ counts as one).
了 is 2 strokes, 女 is 3, 心 is 4, 我 is 7, 妈 is 6. When unsure, look up the stroke-order animation.
Mainland China, Singapore and Malaysia use simplified characters (简体字), with fewer strokes: 国, 学, 马. Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau keep traditional characters (繁體字): 國, 學, 馬.
HanVerse teaches simplified, the standard for daily life in mainland China.
The scripts differ, but Mandarin pronunciation and grammar are the same. Once you read simplified fluently, picking up traditional signs is mostly recognition.
Almost everyone types Chinese by typing pinyin (no letters appear on the keyboard). Type the syllables without tone marks — nihao → a candidate bar shows 你好; tap the number or click the character.
Typing whole words and phrases (beijing, xiexie) is far more accurate than single syllables.
list: nihao → 你好
xieixie → 谢谢
zhongguo → 中国
For ü, type v: nv → 女, lv → 绿

ps: If you don't know a character's pinyin, draw it on the handwriting keyboard or speak it. Both are built into every Chinese phone.

example.py: Wǒ bú huì xiě, dàn huì dǎzì
example.en: I can't write it, but I can type it.

recognizing-signs.title: Reading Real Signs · 招牌识字
recognizing-signs.subtitle: The characters you see on every street.

ps: A handful of characters appear on doors, shops and transport everywhere: 出 exit, 入 enter, 口 opening/mouth, 门 door, 车 vehicle, 站 station, 店 shop, 馆 hall, 局 bureau, 院 institute/hospital.
出口 = exit, 入口 = entrance, 地铁站 = subway station, 卫生间 = restroom.
Combine numbers with 楼 floor and 号 number: 三楼 3rd floor, 五号 No.5, 几号 what number.

example.py: Chūkǒu zài nǎ?
example.en: Where is the exit?

memory-tricks.title: Remembering Characters · 记字技巧
memory-tricks.subtitle: Stories and spacing beat rote repetition.

ps: Turn components into little stories: 忙 busy = heart 忄 + death 亡 ('your heart feels like it's dying = busy'); 休 rest = person 亻 by a tree 木. Vivid images stick far better than stroke count.
Review new characters at increasing intervals (today, tomorrow, in three days, in a week).
Memorize characters inside words and sentences you actually use, not in isolation. 机 appears in 手机 phone, 飞机 plane, 机会 chance — learn all three together.

grammar.title: Grammar Foundations
grammar.subtitle: Word order, 的 and 是 — the frame that every sentence hangs on.

ps: Chinese word order is surprisingly close to English: Subject → Verb → Object. The difference is that Chinese rarely changes this order — there is no conjugation and no tense marking on the verb itself.
What English expresses with word endings ('I walked', 'she eats'), Chinese expresses with small helper words and context. Keep the SVO frame and almost everything else hangs off it.
list: 我 吃 饭 → I eat rice: subject + verb + object
他 喝 茶 → He drinks tea: same frame, no 's' or tense change
你 说 中文 → You speak Chinese
Time phrases go before the verb: 我 明天 去 (I tomorrow go = I'll go tomorrow)

example.py: Wǒ míngtiān qù Běijīng
example.en: I'm going to Beijing tomorrow.

ps: 的 (de) links a word to the thing it describes: my phone, red flowers, the teacher's book. It is the most common character in Chinese and appears everywhere.
Think of it as an invisible 'apostrophe-s' plus 'of': 我的 = my, 妈妈的 = mum's, 红色的 = red-coloured.
list: 我的 手机 → my phone
老师 的 书 → the teacher's book
红色 的 衣服 → red clothes
Skip 的 in fixed daily phrases: 我妈妈 (my mum), not 我的妈妈 — both fine, the short one is natural

example.py: Zhè shì wǒ de péngyou
example.en: This is my friend.

ps: 是 (shì) is 'to be' for linking two things: A is B. It works exactly like 'is' for names, jobs, origins and identities.
It is not used for descriptions the way 'is' is in English — say 我很高兴 (I very happy) without 是. Descriptions just skip the verb.
list: 我 是 老师 → I am a teacher
这 是 什么？ → What is this?
他 是 美国人 → He is American
For feelings use no 是: 我饿 (I'm hungry), 你很漂亮 (you are pretty)

example.zh: 我不是中国人，我是美国人
example.py: Wǒ bú shì Zhōngguó rén, wǒ shì Měiguó rén
example.en: I'm not Chinese, I'm American.

questions.title: Asking Questions
questions.subtitle: The 吗 particle and the six question words that start every conversation.

ps: To turn any statement into a yes/no question, just add 吗 ma at the end. No word order change, no auxiliary verb — one syllable does everything.
This is the single most useful pattern in the language: take a sentence you know, add 吗, and you can ask about anything.
list: 你好 → 你好吗？ (How are you?)
你有钱 → 你有钱吗？ (Do you have money?)
你会中文 → 你会中文吗？ (Do you speak Chinese?)
Answer with the verb: 会 / 不会, 有 / 没有, 是 / 不是

ps: Six question words cover almost every question you will ever need. They sit in the same position the answer would occupy — no inversion, no 'do/does'.
什么 (what), 谁 (who), 哪里/哪儿 (where), 什么时候 (when), 为什么 (why), 怎么 (how).
list: 什么 shénme — what: 这是什么？What is this?
谁 shéi — who: 他是谁？Who is he?
哪里 nǎlǐ / 哪儿 nǎr — where: 厕所在哪里？Where is the toilet?
怎么 zěnme — how: 这个怎么说？How do you say this?

phrases.en: How do I get to the train station?

example.py: Nǐ shénme shíhou lái?
example.en: When are you coming?

ps: 呢 (ne) means 'and you? / what about…?'. After someone answers your question, throw back 你呢 to flip it to them — instant small talk.
It also softens follow-ups: 我的呢？(what about mine?), 明天呢？(and tomorrow?).
list: 我很好，你呢？ → I'm good, and you?
我要咖啡，你呢？ → I'll have coffee, you?
我的手机呢？ → Where's my phone? (what about mine)
Never use 吗 and 呢 together

phrases.py: Nǐ hǎo ma? Wǒ hěn hǎo, nǐ ne?
phrases.en: How are you? I'm great, and you?

measure-words.title: Measure Words
measure-words.subtitle: The little classifiers that count people, books, cups and cars.

ps: In Chinese you cannot just say 'one book' — you must say 'one [classifier] book': 一本书. The classifier matches the category of the thing.
English has a few (a loaf of bread, a pair of shoes); Chinese has one for almost every noun. It sounds strange at first and becomes automatic fast.
list: Pattern: number + measure word + noun — 一 本 书 (one book)
Missing the measure word is the classic foreigner tell
Choose by category: flat things 张, books 本, animals 只, pairs 双
One classifier does most work: 个 (see next section)

ps: 个 (gè) is the default classifier. When you don't know which one to use, 个 is almost always acceptable — people, objects, abstract things.
Master 个 first, then add the specific ones as you meet them. Even native speakers lean on 个 in casual speech.
list: 一个人 → one person
三个苹果 → three apples
这个 → this (one)
几个？ jǐ gè → how many?

example.py: Wǒ yào sān gè bāozi
example.en: I want three buns.

ps: A handful of classifiers cover most everyday nouns. Learning them as pairs ('a cup of…', 'a piece of…') beats memorising lists.
Notice the classifier goes between the number and the noun, and that 两 (liǎng) is used instead of 二 before a classifier: 两个人, never 二个人.
list: 本 běn — for books: 一本书, 两本杂志
张 zhāng — flat things: 一张纸, 一张桌子, 一张票
杯 bēi — drinks: 一杯咖啡, 一杯茶
双 shuāng — pairs: 一双鞋, 一双手

example.py: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi shuǐ
example.en: Please give me a glass of water.

verbs.title: High-Frequency Verbs
verbs.subtitle: 去, 有, 要, 会 and 了 — the verbs that carry 80% of daily talk.

ps: Three verbs do enormous work: 有 yǒu (have/there is), 要 yào (want/need), 会 huì (know how to / can). Together they cover possession, desire and ability.
没有 means 'don't have', 不要 means 'don't want', 不会 means 'can't / don't know how'. Negation is simply 不 or 没 before the verb — no conjugation.
list: 有 yǒu → have: 我有钱 (I have money), 有没有？ (do you have?)
要 yào → want: 我要咖啡 (I want coffee), 不要 (don't want)
会 huì → can: 我会开车 (I can drive), 不会 (can't)
The same verb form works for past, present and future — context does the timing

phrases.en: I want to pay the bill.

sections.h: 去, 来 and 走 — Movement
ps: 去 qù (go), 来 lái (come) and 走 zǒu (leave/walk) are the daily movement verbs. They take a place directly with no preposition: 去北京 = go to Beijing.
The pattern is verb + place: 我去超市 (I go to the supermarket), 你来我家 (you come to my home).
list: 去 qù + place: 去上海, 去机场, 去厕所
来 lái + place: 来中国, 来这儿 (come here)
走 zǒu: 我走了 (I'm leaving / gotta go)
Asking direction: 怎么去？ (how to get there?)

phrases.en: Are you coming to my place?

example.py: Zěnme qù huǒchēzhàn?
example.en: How do I get to the train station?

ps: 了 (le) after a verb marks that something happened or is complete: 我吃了 (I ate), 他来了 (he has come). It is Chinese's closest thing to a past tense.
For actions you did in the past with no special emphasis, 了 is often left out in conversation. Use it when the completion matters: 我买了两杯咖啡.
list: Verb + 了 = completed action: 吃了, 去了, 看了
吃了饭 → ate (the meal)
他来了 → he has arrived
Don't force it: 昨天我去公园 is fine without 了 — completion isn't always marked

example.py: Wǒ mǎi le liǎng bēi kāfēi
example.en: I bought two cups of coffee.

negation.title: 不 vs. 没 · 两种否定
negation.subtitle: 不 negates habits and the future; 没 negates completed facts.

ps: 不 negates regular actions, things you won't do, and adjectival states: 我不喝咖啡 I don't drink coffee; 今天不去 I won't go today.
It pairs with 是, 想, 会, 喜欢 and most verbs of attitude.
没 (or 没有) negates things that did or didn't happen, and possession: 我没去 I didn't go; 我没有钱 I don't have money. With action verbs in the past, use 没 + verb (never 不).

example.zh: 我不喝咖啡，今天也没买
example.py: Wǒ bù hē kāfēi, jīntiān yě méi mǎi
example.en: I don't drink coffee, and didn't buy any today.

de-di-de.title: 的 地 得 · Three 'de'
de-di-de.subtitle: Possession, adverbs, and complements use three different characters.

sections.h: 的 for nouns, 地 for verbs
ps: 的 links a description to a noun: 红色的花 red flowers, 我的书 my book. 地 links an adverb to a verb: 慢慢地说 speak slowly, 认真地学 study carefully.
Both sound like 'de' — the character tells you the grammar.
得 follows a verb or adjective to add a result or degree: 说得好 speak well, 跑得快 run fast, 好得很 extremely good. Pattern: verb + 得 + comment.

example.py: Tā pǎo de hěn kuài
example.en: He runs very fast.

you-have.title: The Verb 有 · 拥有
you-have.subtitle: Have, exist — and how to negate it.

ps: 有 means both 'to have' and 'there is/exists': 我有时间 I have time; 附近有药店 there's a pharmacy nearby. It is negated with 没 (没有), never 不有.
Questions use 有没有: 你有没有现金? Do you have cash?
有 + time/amount means 'a certain' or 'some': 有一天 one day, 有一次 once, 有人 someone.
在 locates someone/something: 我在北京 I'm in Beijing; 书在桌子上 the book is on the table. Place words often end in 上/下/里/旁边.
Ask where with 在哪: 卫生间在哪? Where is the restroom?

phrases.en: The keys are in the bag.

ps: 在 before an action means '-ing' right now: 我在吃饭 I'm eating; 他们在开会 they're in a meeting. Add 正在 for emphasis.

example.py: Tā zài jiǔdiàn xiūxi
example.en: He's resting at the hotel.

le.title: 了 · Change & Completion
le.subtitle: 了 marks completed actions and new situations.

ps: 了 after a verb shows the action happened or is completed: 我吃了 I ate; 我买了一张票 I bought a ticket. It is not a fixed past tense — it works in future clauses too (你到了给我电话 call me when you arrive).
Negating a completed action uses 没, and 了 usually drops: 我没吃 I didn't eat.
At the end, 了 signals a new situation or 'now it's so': 下雨了 it's raining (now); 我懂了 I get it now; 没有了 there's none left.

example.py: Wǒ chī le liǎng wǎn fàn, bǎo le
example.en: I ate two bowls and I'm full now.

ps: 过 after a verb means you have had the experience: 我去过中国 I've been to China; 你吃过臭豆腐吗? Have you ever eaten stinky tofu?
It focuses on the experience, not a specific time — contrast with 了 (a specific completion).
To say you've never done something: 我没吃过 I've never eaten it. 过 stays, unlike with 了.

example.zh: 我去过上海，没去过广州
example.py: Wǒ qùguo Shànghǎi, méi qùguo Guǎngzhōu
example.en: I've been to Shanghai, not Guangzhou.

zhe.title: 着 · Ongoing State
zhe.subtitle: The window is open, he is wearing a coat.

ps: 着 shows an action's result is still in effect: 门开着 the door is open; 他穿着外套 he's wearing a coat; 桌上放着书 there's a book lying on the table.
It's common for posture and placement: 坐着 sit, 站着 stand, 躺着 lie.

phrases.en: A map hangs on the wall.

ps: For 'right in the middle of doing', combine 正在…(呢): 他们正在开会呢 they're having a meeting right now.

example.py: Diàn lǐ fàngzhe yīnyuè
example.en: Music is playing in the shop.

zhengzai.title: 正在 · In Progress
zhengzai.subtitle: The Chinese '-ing' for actions happening now.

ps: Mark present continuous three ways: 在 + verb (我在做饭), 正在 + verb (我正在做饭), or add 呢 at the end (我做饭呢). They are interchangeable in daily speech.
Unlike English, there is no verb ending — only these helper words.
你在干什么? What are you doing? — a very common, casual line.

example.py: Tā zhèngzài kāihuì, děng yíxià
example.en: He's in a meeting, wait a moment.

modal-verbs.title: 会 能 可以 · Can & May
modal-verbs.subtitle: Three ways to say 'can' — skill, ability, permission.

sections.h: 会 = learned skill; 能 = ability/circumstance
ps: 会 is a skill you learned: 我会说中文 I can speak Chinese. 能 is being able given ability or conditions: 你能来吗? Can you make it? 我今天不能喝酒 I can't drink today.
Both translate as 'can', but 会 stresses know-how, 能 stresses possibility.
可以 asks or grants permission: 我可以进来吗? May I come in? 可以! Sure/you may. It also means 'feasible'.

example.zh: 我会一点中文，可以自己点菜
example.py: Wǒ huì yìdiǎnr Zhōngwén, kěyǐ zìjǐ diǎn cài
example.en: I know some Chinese, so I can order myself.

want-verbs.title: 要 想 希望 · Want
want-verbs.subtitle: From firm intention to gentle wishes.

ps: 想 is 'would like / want to' (mild): 我想去 I'd like to go. 要 is stronger — 'want to / am going to': 我要这个 I want this one; often used for orders: 我要一杯咖啡 I'll have a coffee.
想 + verb also means 'to miss' with a person: 我想家 I miss home.

phrases.en: I'll have a bowl of noodles.

sections.h: 打算 / 希望 for plans and hopes
ps: 打算 is 'plan to' (我打算来 I plan to come); 希望 is 'hope' (希望能见到你 hope to see you).

example.zh: 我想学，但是现在要工作
example.py: Wǒ xiǎng xué, dànshì xiànzài yào gōngzuò
example.en: I'd like to study, but I have to work now.

hen-adj.title: 很 + Adjective · 很
hen-adj.subtitle: Chinese adjectives don't take 是, and 很 is often just a filler.

ps: You don't say 我是忙 (I am busy); say 我很忙. Chinese adjectives directly follow the subject, and 很 (hěn) usually links them — but it often carries little 'very' meaning, just filling the slot.
Negate with 不: 不忙 not busy.
To really grade an adjective use 非常 very, 特别 especially, 比较 relatively, 有点 a bit, 太…了 too…: 有点贵 a bit pricey; 太好了! great!

example.zh: 这个房间有点小，但是很干净
example.py: Zhège fángjiān yǒudiǎnr xiǎo, dànshì hěn gānjìng
example.en: This room is a bit small but very clean.

adverbs.title: 也 都 才 就 还 · Common Adverbs
adverbs.subtitle: Small words that carry the logic.

ps: 也 adds 'also': 我也去 I'm going too. 都 means 'all/already' and sits before the verb: 我们都去 we're all going; 都八点了 it's already 8.
Question words + 都 mean 'every/any': 都可以 anything is fine; 谁都知道 everyone knows.

sections.h: 才 only/late, 就 early/then, 还 still
ps: 才 shows something happens late or is small (才来 just arrived, 五十块 only 50); 就 shows earliness or consequence (八点就来 came as early as 8); 还 means still (还在 still here).

example.py: Yí gè jiù gòu le, búyòng dōu mǎi
example.en: One is enough, no need to buy all.

conjunctions.title: 和 还是 或者 · And / Or
conjunctions.subtitle: Different 'or's for statements vs. questions.

ps: 和 (hé) links nouns and pronouns: 我和你 you and me, 咖啡和茶 coffee and tea. It usually does not link full sentences the way English 'and' does — clauses are often just placed in sequence.
跟 and 同 work like 和 in casual speech.

phrases.en: Both tea and coffee are available.

sections.h: 还是 for questions, 或者 for statements
ps: In questions offering choices use 还是: 咖啡还是茶? Coffee or tea? In statements use 或者: 咖啡或者茶都行 coffee or tea is fine.

phrases.py: Nǐ hē shuǐ háishì hē chá?
phrases.en: Will you drink water or tea?

example.zh: 你要现金或者扫码都行
example.py: Nǐ yào xiànjīn huòzhě sǎomǎ dōu xíng
example.en: Cash or scanning, either works for you.

bi.title: 比 · Comparisons
bi.subtitle: A 比 B + adjective — the core comparison pattern.

ps: Chinese compares with A 比 B + adjective: 今天比昨天热 today is hotter than yesterday. Do not add 很 in this pattern — say 他比我高, not 比我很高.
Add degree with 一点 a bit, 得多 a lot, 更 even.

phrases.en: The subway is faster than a taxi.
He's a little taller than me.

ps: A 没有 B + adj means A is not as… as B (我没有他高 I'm not as tall as him). 不如 is a concise alternative: 这个不如那个好 this isn't as good as that.

phrases.en: I'm not as busy as you.
Walking isn't as good as taking a ride.

example.py: Wēixìn bǐ xiànjīn fāngbiàn de duō
example.en: WeChat is far more convenient than cash.

ba.title: 把字句 · The 把 Sentence
ba.subtitle: Move the object up front when you dispose of or change it.

ps: The 把 structure moves the object before the verb to emphasize what happens TO it: subject + 把 + object + verb + result. 我把饭吃完了 I finished the rice (literally 'took the rice and ate it finished').
It usually needs a result, location or 了 — a bare verb rarely works.
把 is everywhere in chores and handling things: 把衣服洗了 do the laundry, 把房间打扫一下 clean the room, 把这个打包 pack this.

example.py: Qǐng bǎ zhàngdān gěi wǒ
example.en: Please bring me the bill.

bei.title: 被字句 · The 被 Sentence
bei.subtitle: Passive voice for things that happen to you.

ps: 被 introduces the doer in a passive sentence, often for mishaps: 我的钱包被偷了 my wallet was stolen; 杯子被他打破了 the cup was broken by him.
In casual speech 叫 or 让 replace 被. When the doer is unknown you can omit it: 被偷了 got stolen.

phrases.py: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le

phrases.en: He got caught in the rain.

sections.h: Not every English passive uses 被
ps: Chinese prefers active wording for neutral things: 会议取消了 the meeting was cancelled (no 被 needed). Reserve 被 mainly for affected/adverse events.

phrases.en: The food is ready (lit. cooked done).

example.py: Wǒ de xínglǐ bèi nònghuài le
example.en: My luggage got damaged.

resultative.title: Result Complements · 结果补语
resultative.subtitle: Verb + result: did it actually get done?

sections.h: Attach the outcome to the verb
ps: Chinese packs the result right after the verb: 听懂 listen-understand = catch what's said; 看见 look-see = see; 吃完 eat-finish; 找到 search-arrive = find; 写错 write-wrong.
The potential forms 看得见/看不见 express can/can't achieve the result.
完 finish, 好 done/set, 到 attained, 见 perceived, 懂 understood, 对 correct, 错 wrong, 开 open, 关 closed, 住 fixed/held — combine freely with action verbs.

example.py: Wǒ méi tīngqīng, qǐng zài shuō yí biàn
example.en: I didn't hear clearly, please say it again.

directional.title: Directional Complements · 趋向补语
directional.subtitle: 来/去 and up-down-in-out show movement direction.

sections.h: 来 toward the speaker, 去 away
ps: Attach 来 if movement is toward you, 去 if away: 过来 come over, 进去 go in, 回来 come back, 上去 go up. The direction is from the speaker's viewpoint.
Combine with position verbs: 上/下/进/出/回/过/起 + 来/去.
Some directional complements become idiomatic: 想起来 remember (lit. rise up), 看起来 it looks like, 听下去 keep listening.

example.py: Tā xià lóu qù mǎi shuǐ le
example.en: He went downstairs to buy water.

shi-de.title: 是…的 · Emphasizing Details
shi-de.subtitle: Highlight when, where or how something happened.

ps: To emphasize the time, place or manner of a past event, wrap it with 是…的: 我是昨天来的 it was yesterday that I came; 我是在北京认识他的 it was in Beijing that I met him.
The object can sit before 的: 我是去年买的房子.

phrases.py: Wǒ shì zuò fēijī lái de

ps: Use 了 just to state an action happened; use 是…的 when the point is the detail (when/where/how).

phrases.en: It was in the morning that he left.

example.py: Wǒ shì zài Shànghǎi xué de Zhōngwén
example.en: It was in Shanghai that I learned Chinese.

ps: State the condition with 如果 (if), then the result with 就 (then): 如果下雨，我就不去 if it rains, I won't go. 就 is often the real marker; 如果 can be dropped.
For 'as long as', use 只要…就; for 'only if', 只有…才.

phrases.py: Rúguǒ nǐ máng, jiù suàn le

ps: Tag a clause with 的话 to mean 'in the case of': 有空的话 if you're free; 不行的话 if that doesn't work.

phrases.en: Tell me if you need it.

phrases.py: Bù guì de huà wǒ jiù mǎi
phrases.en: If it's cheap I'll buy it.

example.py: Bú huì de huà, jiù wèn fúwùyuán
example.en: If you can't, just ask the waiter.

ps: Because pairs with therefore: 因为下雨，所以我没去 because it rained, I didn't go. In short sentences either word can be dropped, but Chinese does NOT stack 'because…although' the way English might.
Since/既然 works for 'given that': 既然来了就别走了.

phrases.en: There was traffic, so I was late.

phrases.py: Tā bìng le, suǒyǐ méi lái
phrases.en: He was sick, so he didn't come.

ps: Although pairs with but: 虽然贵，但是好用 although expensive, it works well. In Chinese you CAN keep both 虽然 and 但是 (English keeps only one).

example.zh: 因为便宜，所以买了两个
example.py: Yīnwèi piányi, suǒyǐ mǎi le liǎng gè
example.en: They were cheap, so I bought two.

ps: Same: A 跟 B 一样 (A is the same as B). Add an adjective: 他跟我一样高 he's as tall as me. Negate with 不: 跟这个不一样 it's different from this one.
差不多 means 'about the same'.

phrases.en: This one is the same as that.
The prices are about the same.

phrases.py: Wǒ de gēn nǐ de bù yíyàng

ps: 像 means 'looks like/resembles': 他像他爸爸 he looks like his dad; 像真的一样 looks almost real.

example.zh: 这个发音跟那个一样吗？
example.py: Zhège fāyīn gēn nàge yíyàng ma?
example.en: Is this pronunciation the same as that one?

numbers.title: Numbers
numbers.subtitle: Count, price and phone numbers from zero to 万.

ps: Chinese numbers are very regular once you know 0-10. Everything above ten is built by combining these.
Note the tone on yī changes by sandhi, but the base form is yī.
list: 0 líng 零 / 1 yī 一 / 2 èr 二
3 sān 三 / 4 sì 四 / 5 wǔ 五
6 liù 六 / 7 qī 七 / 8 bā 八 / 9 jiǔ 九 / 10 shí 十

ps: 11 is 'ten-one' (十一), 12 is 'ten-two' (十二). 20 is 'two-ten' (二十), 21 is 'two-ten-one' (二十一). It is beautifully logical.
100 is 一百 yì bǎi, and the big unit you must know is 万 wàn = ten thousand (a new step, not a 'thousand').
list: 11 shí yī / 15 shí wǔ / 19 shí jiǔ
20 èr shí / 21 èr shí yī / 99 jiǔ shí jiǔ
100 yì bǎi / 1,000 yì qiān
10,000 yì wàn (ten thousand — remember 万 = 10,000, not 1,000)

example.py: sān shí wǔ
example.en: thirty-five

ps: In daily life people rarely say 元 yuán. They say 块 kuài for the whole yuan, 毛 máo for ten cents, and 分 fēn for one cent.
A price like 12.5 yuan is spoken as 'twelve kuai five', skipping the decimal point entirely.

sections.h: Phone Numbers and the yāo Rule
ps: When reading out a phone number, people say the digits one by one. Crucially, a 1 inside a number is often read as yāo rather than yī, to avoid confusion with 7 (qī) over a bad line.
So 138 is pronounced yāo sān bā, not yī sān bā.
list: 1 in a phone number often reads yāo
138 → yāo sān bā
Read numbers digit by digit, not as a whole number
Write it down if unsure: 1 and 7 sound similar on the phone

example.py: Wǒ de diànhuà shì yāo sān bā
example.en: My phone number is 138.

time.title: Time & Dates
time.subtitle: Clock times, days and dates — 'what time' is one of your first real conversations.

sections.h: Clock Time: 点 and 分
ps: Hours are 点 diǎn, minutes are 分 fēn. To say 3:15 you literally say 'three o'clock fifteen minutes': 三点十五 (sān diǎn shíwǔ).
To ask the time, use 几 (jǐ, 'how many') — 几点？ (What time?). Half past is 半 bàn: 三点半 = 3:30.
list: 一点 yī diǎn → 1:00
三点半 sān diǎn bàn → 3:30
六点十分 liù diǎn shí fēn → 6:10
现在几点？ Xiànzài jǐ diǎn? → What time is it now?

example.py: Wǒ qī diǎn qǐchuáng
example.en: I get up at 7.

ps: Days are built on 星期 xīngqī (week): Monday is 'week one', Tuesday 'week two', up to Sunday 'week day' (星期日 or 星期天).
Monday is the first day in China's convention: 星期一, not Sunday. Remembering 一 to 日 makes all seven days instant.
list: 星期一 xīngqī yī → Monday
星期二 xīngqī èr → Tuesday … 星期六 xīngqī liù → Saturday
星期日 / 星期天 xīngqī rì / tiān → Sunday
今天 jīntiān today / 明天 míngtiān tomorrow / 昨天 zuótiān yesterday

ps: Months are simply numbers in front of 月 yuè: January is 一月 ('month one'), December is 十二月. Dates put the day number after 号 hào (or 日 rì).
Full date order is year → month → day: 2026年10月7日 — always biggest unit first, like addresses.
list: 一月 yī yuè January / 十月 shí yuè October
今天几号？ Jīntiān jǐ hào? → What's the date today?
十月七号 shí yuè qī hào → October 7th
Year first: 二〇二六年十月 → October 2026

phrases.py: Wǒ de shēngrì shì bā yuè

example.py: Wǒ shí yuè qī hào dào Shànghǎi
example.en: I arrive in Shanghai on October 7th.

family.title: Family & Titles
family.subtitle: Who is who at home, and how to address people politely outside it.

ps: Chinese family words are precise about age and side of the family — 哥哥 is an older brother, 弟弟 a younger one. Get the pattern and the whole tree opens up.
Start with the immediate circle: 爸爸 dad, 妈妈 mum, 哥哥 older brother, 姐姐 older sister, 弟弟 younger brother, 妹妹 younger sister.
list: 爸爸 bàba / 妈妈 māma — dad / mum
哥哥 gēge / 弟弟 dìdi — older / younger brother
姐姐 jiějie / 妹妹 mèimei — older / younger sister
Add 的 to say 'my': 我妈妈 (my mum), 我哥哥 (my older brother)

phrases.py: Nǐ jiā lǐ yǒu jǐ gè rén?
phrases.en: How many people are in your family?

ps: Addressing strangers politely is a key Chinese skill. Use title + surname, never a first name for someone senior or unfamiliar.
老师 (teacher), 先生 (Mr), 女士 (Ms/Mrs) and 师傅 (master worker — for drivers, cooks, tradespeople) are your daily titles.
list: 王老师 Wáng lǎoshī → Teacher Wang (any professional you respect)
李先生 Lǐ xiānsheng → Mr Li
张女士 Zhāng nǚshì → Ms Zhang
师傅 shīfu → for taxi drivers, repair people, chefs

survival.title: Survival Phrases
survival.subtitle: Fifteen sentences you can use the moment you land.

ps: Memorise these fifteen. They cover greetings, thanks, emergencies, shopping, asking for help and saying goodbye — everything a beginner needs on day one.
Don't worry about perfect tones yet; saying these slowly and clearly will get you understood.
对不起 (Duìbuqǐ) is for a real apology or to squeeze past someone — like 'excuse me / sorry'. It is paired with 没关系 (Méi guānxi), the standard 'it's nothing, don't worry about it' reply.
Adding 请 qǐng (please) to any sentence instantly sounds more polite. Use it with requests: 请再说一遍, 请给我...
list: Bump into someone → say 对不起; they answer 没关系
Don't understand → say 我不明白, then 请再说一遍
Add 请 qǐng to be polite: 请再说一遍, 请给我杯水
Hello to a group: 你们好 (Nǐmen hǎo), not just 你好

ps: When you finish a meal, wave and say 买单 (mǎi dān) — that is how you ask for the bill, not the English 'check please'.
For urgent help, 救命! (Jiùmìng!) is the real cry for help; use 我迷路了 (I'm lost) with a map or a friendly local.
list: Asking for the bill → wave and say 买单
Asking the price → 多少钱？ or 这个怎么卖？
Hungry and need food → 我饿了 + point at a menu
Genuinely in danger → shout 救命！; otherwise 请帮帮我 (please help me)

greetings-sent.title: Greeting Lines · 问候句型
greetings-sent.subtitle: Hello, goodbye and the natural replies.

ps: Open with 你好 (or the time-based 早上好/下午好/晚上好). Part with 再见, or warmer 回头见 see you later / 明天见 see you tomorrow. Welcome someone with 欢迎!
Reply to 你好 simply with 你好; to 谢谢 with 不客气/不谢; to 对不起 with 没关系.
Before asking a stranger, lead with 请问 (qǐngwèn, 'may I ask') — it makes any question polite: 请问，卫生间在哪?

example.zh: 你好，请问地铁站怎么走？

example.en: Hello, how do I get to the subway station?

我是老师/工程师/学生 I'm a teacher/engineer/student; 我在…工作 I work at…; 我在学中文 I'm learning Chinese.

polite-sent.title: Polite Phrases · 礼貌用语
polite-sent.subtitle: The ten lines that smooth every interaction.

ps: 谢谢 / 非常感谢 thanks; 不客气 you're welcome. 对不起 / 不好意思 sorry (excuse me); 没关系 it's fine. 麻烦你了 sorry to trouble you; 辛苦了 thanks for the effort (to staff/drivers).
不好意思 is the workhorse for squeezing past, getting attention or a light apology.
请 + action softens a request: 请帮我 please help me, 请等一下 please wait, 请再说一遍 please say it again, 请慢一点 please (speak/go) slower.

phrases.py: Qǐng zài shuō yí biàn hǎo ma?

ps: Signal staff: 服务员! Ask for the menu: 请给我菜单. Order: 我要… / 来一份… / 这个来一份. State preferences: 不要辣/不要香菜. Add: 再来一瓶水.
If unsure: 有什么推荐? What do you recommend?

phrases.zh: 我要这个，这个，还有这个。
phrases.py: Wǒ yào zhège, zhège, hái yǒu zhège.
phrases.en: I'll have this, this, and this.

ps: Ask for things: 请加一双筷子 chopsticks, 拿张纸巾 napkin. Compliment: 很好吃! Settle: 买单/结账, and 请打包 to box leftovers.

example.zh: 服务员，来两碗牛肉面，不要香菜，再来一瓶水。
example.py: Fúwùyuán, lái liǎng wǎn niúròu miàn, bú yào xiāngcài, zài lái yì píng shuǐ.

ps: Wave off help politely: 我随便看看 I'm just looking. Ask about stock: 这个有…号/颜色吗? Request to try: 可以试穿吗? Ask about price: 这个多少钱?
Bargain gently: 能便宜一点吗? / 太贵了.

phrases.en: Do you have one size up?
Can you come down a bit?
Let me look a bit more.

ps: Decide: 就这个吧 I'll take this. Ask where to pay: 在哪付钱? Request receipt: 能开发票吗? Refuse a bag: 不用袋子.

example.zh: 这个有中号吗？……好，就这个，能开发票吗？
example.py: Zhège yǒu zhōng hào ma? …… Hǎo, jiù zhège, néng kāi fāpiào ma?
example.en: Do you have this in medium? … OK, I'll take it — can I get a fapiao?

directions-sent.title: Asking the Way · 问路句型
directions-sent.subtitle: Get directions and confirm you understood.

ps: Lead with 请问, then 请问…怎么走? / …在哪? / 附近有…吗? Ask distance/time: 离这儿远吗? 走路几分钟? 要坐几站?
Name the place clearly; showing the address in Chinese on your phone helps.

phrases.py: Nǐ néng zhǐ gěi wǒ kàn ma?
phrases.en: Can you show me (on the map)?

ps: Listen for 直走 straight, 左转/右转 turn, 在…路口 at the intersection, 过了… past…, 就在…旁边/对面 next to/across from. Confirm: 是这边吗? Is it this way?

example.zh: 请问人民广场怎么走？直走，在第二个路口右转吗？
example.py: Qǐngwèn Rénmín Guǎngchǎng zěnme zǒu? Yìzhí zǒu, zài dì-èr gè lùkǒu yòu zhuǎn ma?
example.en: How do I get to People's Square? Straight, then turn right at the second intersection?

taxi-sent.title: Taxi Lines · 打车句型
taxi-sent.subtitle: Tell the driver where and how.

ps: 师傅 (shīfu) is the polite way to address a driver. State the destination: 师傅，我去… / 请到…. Show the Chinese address if needed. Ask the meter: 请打表.
Ask time/price: 大概多久? 大概多少钱?

phrases.en: Driver, I'm going to the train station.

ps: Ask to hurry: 我赶时间，请快一点. Stop: 请在前面停 / 在这儿停. Ask to be alerted: 到了叫我一声. Pay via QR or cash.

phrases.en: Please stop at the intersection ahead.

example.zh: 师傅，我去机场，我赶时间，请走最快的路。
example.py: Shīfu, wǒ qù jīchǎng, wǒ gǎn shíjiān, qǐng zǒu zuì kuài de lù.
example.en: Driver, to the airport — I'm in a hurry, please take the fastest route.

ps: 我预订了房间 I've booked a room; give your name/passport: 这是我的护照. Ask WiFi: WiFi密码是多少? Request things: 能给我…吗? Ask breakfast/check-out times.
Room issues: …坏了 …is broken; 请派人来修 please send someone.

phrases.py: Wǒ yùdìng le fángjiān, xìng Smith.
phrases.en: I have a reservation, under Smith.

ps: Late check-out: 能延迟退房吗? Store bags: 能寄存行李吗? Wake-up call: 请明早六点叫我. Settle: 我要退房.

phrases.en: Can I leave my luggage here?

phrases.py: Qǐng duō gěi yì tiáo bèizi.
Qǐng míngzǎo liù diǎn jiàoxǐng wǒ.

example.zh: 你好，我要退房，能帮我叫辆出租车吗？
example.py: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ yào tuìfáng, néng bāng wǒ jiào liàng chūzūchē ma?
example.en: Hi, I'm checking out — could you call me a taxi?

bank-post.title: Bank & Post Office · 银行邮局
bank-post.subtitle: Money, cards and sending things.

ps: 我想换钱 I'd like to change money; specify: 换人民币 into RMB, 换美元 into dollars. ATM: 在哪取钱? Card problems: 我的卡被吞了 the ATM ate my card.
Open an account: 我想办张银行卡.

phrases.en: I'd like to change some RMB.

phrases.py: Wǒ de kǎ bèi tūn le.

phrases.en: I'd like to open a card.

ps: 我想寄快递 I want to send a package; 寄到… send to…; ask about cost and time: 多少钱? 几天到? Track: 帮我查个快递.

phrases.en: I'd like to send a package.

example.zh: 你好，我想把这个包裹寄到美国，几天能到？
example.py: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ xiǎng bǎ zhège bāoguǒ jì dào Měiguó, jǐ tiān néng dào?
example.en: Hi, I'd like to send this package to the US — how many days?

emergency-sent.title: Emergency Lines · 紧急句型
emergency-sent.subtitle: The sentences you hope never to need.

ps: 救命! Help! 帮帮我! Help me! 请报警 call the police; 请叫救护车 call an ambulance; 请带我去医院 take me to hospital. Point to injuries: 我…受伤了 / 这儿疼.
Lost documents: 我的护照丢了; stolen: 我的钱包被偷了.

phrases.py: Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le.

ps: 我需要帮助 I need help; 请联系大使馆/领事馆 contact the embassy/consulate; 我是外国人 I'm a foreigner; 能说英语吗? is there an English speaker? Keep scanned copies of your passport separately.

phrases.en: I'd like to file a report.

phrases.py: Yǒu rén néng shuō Yīngyǔ ma?

example.zh: 帮帮我，我的护照丢了，请帮我联系大使馆。
example.py: Bāngbang wǒ, wǒ de hùzhào diū le, qǐng bāng wǒ liánxì dàshǐguǎn.
example.en: Help me — I've lost my passport; please contact the embassy for me.

phone-sent.title: On the Phone · 电话沟通
phone-sent.subtitle: Answering, holding and confirming.

ps: 喂 (wéi) opens a phone call. Identify yourself: 我是… (this is…). Ask for someone: 请问…在吗? If wrong number: 你打错了 you have the wrong number.
Ask them to wait: 请稍等 please hold; ask them to repeat: 你说什么? 信号不好.

phrases.py: Xìnhào bù hǎo, tīng bù qīng.
phrases.en: Bad signal, I can't hear clearly.

ps: Confirm details: 我的电话是… my number is…; 我们…见 let's meet at…; close with 好，再见 / 到时候见.

phrases.py: Nǐ néng fā duǎnxìn gěi wǒ ma?

phrases.en: OK, let's leave it at that.

example.zh: 喂你好，我是 Tom，请问李医生在吗？信号不太好，请大声一点。
example.py: Wéi nǐ hǎo, wǒ shì Tom, qǐngwèn Lǐ yīshēng zài ma? Xìnhào bú tài hǎo, qǐng dàshēng yìdiǎnr.
example.en: Hello, this is Tom — is Dr. Li there? The signal is weak, please speak up.

small-talk.title: Small Talk · 寒暄闲聊
small-talk.subtitle: The safe, friendly lines Chinese people use.

ps: 你吃了吗? 'Have you eaten?' is a warm greeting, not an invitation — answer 吃了，你呢? Other safe topics: 你是哪国人? where are you from; 你来中国多久了? how long have you been here; 你做什么工作? what do you do.
Avoid money, age and politics with new acquaintances.

phrases.py: Nǐ lái Zhōngguó duō jiǔ le?
phrases.en: How long have you been in China?

phrases.py: Wǒ lái le yí gè yuè.

phrases.en: Have you gotten used to it?

ps: Accept compliments by deflecting modestly: 哪里哪里 / 没有没有. Praise the food/host: 菜很好吃; 你太客气了 you're too kind. Say cheers: 干杯!

phrases.py: Nǐ Zhōngwén shuō de zhēn hǎo!
Nǎlǐ nǎlǐ, hái chà de yuǎn.
phrases.en: Oh not at all, far from it.

example.zh: 你吃了吗？吃了，谢谢，你呢？菜太好吃了！
example.py: Nǐ chī le ma? Chī le, xièxie, nǐ ne? Cài tài hǎochī le!
example.en: Have you eaten? Yes thanks, you? The food is wonderful!

travel-check.title: Airport & Border Lines · 机场海关
travel-check.subtitle: Check-in, security and customs.

ps: 我要办理值机 I'd like to check in; 靠窗/靠过道的座位 a window/aisle seat; 这个随身带 I'll carry this on; 这个托运 check this bag. At security: 需要拿出电脑吗?
Boarding: 登机口在哪? 几点登机?

phrases.py: Yǒu kào chuāng de zuòwèi ma?

ps: Common questions: 你来做什么? purpose (旅游/商务/学习); 待多久? how long; 住在哪里? where staying. Have your passport, return ticket and hotel address ready.

example.zh: 你好，我来旅游，待十天，住在市中心的酒店。
example.py: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ lái lǚyóu, dāi shí tiān, zhù zài shì zhōngxīn de jiǔdiàn.
example.en: Hello, I'm here as a tourist for ten days, staying at a city-center hotel.

culture-traps.title: Culture Traps
culture-traps.subtitle: The mistakes foreigners make without realising it.

ps: Language and culture go together. These small mismatches cause more confusion than grammar ever will.
Reading this list once will save you several awkward moments in your first weeks.
list: Tipping: China has no tipping culture — leaving money on the table can confuse or even offend; just pay the bill as printed.
'Yes' doesn't always mean yes: a nod or 好 hǎo often means 'I hear you', not 'I agree', and direct refusal is often softened.
Names: do not call elders, teachers or bosses by their first name; use title + surname, e.g. 王老师 Teacher Wang.
Greeting: greetings are usually a handshake, a nod or a small bow — hugs and kisses on the cheek are not expected.
'Gan bei' means 'dry the glass': in a toast you may take a small sip; you don't have to empty the glass unless you choose to.
Being 'loud' or arguing: saving face matters; criticism is usually delivered softly in private, so a calm tone wins.

ps: Sound and colour carry real meaning in daily life, from elevators to wedding decorations.
These are superstitions, not rules — but noticing them makes you look attentive.
list: The number 4 sì sounds like death sǐ, so buildings often skip the 4th floor (like some Western buildings skip the 13th).
Red is lucky: red envelopes (红包 hóngbāo), red banners and red clothing at weddings mean joy and good fortune, not danger.

ps: A few gift choices and table gestures are deeply loaded. Small slips here can spoil an otherwise kind gesture.
When in doubt, tea, fruit or nice snacks are safe, friendly gifts.
list: Bad gifts: giving a clock (送钟 sòng zhōng) sounds like 'attending a funeral', pears (梨 lí) and umbrellas (伞 sǎn) sound like 'parting' — avoid them as gifts.
Chopsticks: never stick chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice — it resembles a funeral ritual and is deeply unlucky.

names-titles.title: Names & Forms of Address · 姓名称呼
names-titles.subtitle: How Chinese names and titles work.

ps: Chinese names put the family name first: in 王小明, 王 is the surname and 小明 the given name. Address strangers or elders by surname + title: 王先生 Mr. Wang, 李小姐 Ms. Li, 张师傅 skilled worker/driver 张.
Using just the given name signals closeness and usually comes after invitation.
In shops and restaurants use 服务员; for drivers and repair workers 师傅 is warm and respectful; an older neighbor can be 阿姨 (auntie) or 叔叔 (uncle) even if unrelated.
Use 你 (nǐ) with friends and peers, but switch to the polite 您 (nín) for elders, strangers, doctors and formal service — 您好! is the respectful hello.

example.zh: 您好，请问您贵姓？……王女士，您好。
example.py: Nín hǎo, qǐngwèn nín guì xìng? …… Wáng nǚshì, nín hǎo.
example.en: Hello, may I ask your surname? … Ms. Wang, nice to meet you.

face.title: Face · 面子
face.subtitle: Reputation, dignity and keeping things smooth.

ps: 面子 (miànzi) is social dignity and standing. Praising someone publicly 给面子 gives face; openly correcting, embarrassing or losing your temper makes them 丢面子 lose face.
Disagreements and complaints are best delivered gently, in private, with a way for the other person to save face.

phrases.en: to show you respect / do it for your sake
save a little face for someone
He was very gracious/showed real respect

ps: Avoid flat 'no' and public arguments; phrase refusals as 我再看看 / 可能不太方便. Compliment genuinely, and let hosts treat you without a loud fight over the bill.

phrases.en: Let me think about it (a soft no).

example.zh: （不当众指责）这个我们私下聊好吗？
example.py: （bù dāngzhòng zhǐzé）Zhège wǒmen sīxià liáo hǎo ma?
example.en: (Avoid public criticism) Shall we talk about this privately?

guanxi.title: Relationships · 关系
guanxi.subtitle: The network of mutual help that gets things done.

ps: 关系 (guānxi) is the ongoing web of personal relationships and mutual obligations through which favors, introductions and trust flow. It is built over time by reliability, meals and small helps — not one-off transactions.
A warm introduction (介绍) from a mutual friend opens doors that cold calls do not.

phrases.en: ask a friend for a favor

ps: Favors create 人情 (rénqíng), a social debt people repay later. Accept help warmly, say thanks, and look for chances to give back — but don't treat friendship as purely transactional.

phrases.en: I'll treat you to a meal later.

example.zh: 这次谢谢你帮忙，改天我请你吃饭。
example.py: Zhè cì xièxie nǐ bāngmáng, gǎitiān wǒ qǐng nǐ chīfàn.
example.en: Thanks for the help this time — I'll treat you to a meal another day.

keqi.title: Politeness · 客气
keqi.subtitle: Being a considerate guest and customer.

ps: 客气 (kèqi) means being courteous and not imposing. Guests initially decline offers (客气一下) before accepting; hosts keep offering. Don't grab the best seat or pour only your own tea.
When someone thanks you, 不客气 ('don't be polite') means you're welcome.

phrases.en: Make yourself at home / you're welcome.

ps: Tap two fingers when tea is poured to say thanks; pour tea for others before yourself; the host may pay the bill after a token, friendly tussle — let them if they insist and repay next time.

example.zh: （轻叩两指）谢谢，您别忙了，我自己来。
example.py: （qīng kòu liǎng zhǐ）Xièxie, nín bié máng le, wǒ zìjǐ lái.
example.en: (Tap two fingers) Thanks, please don't fuss — I'll help myself.

taboos-words.title: Word Taboos & Homophones · 语言禁忌
taboos-words.subtitle: Sounds that carry bad luck — and how to avoid them.

ps: Because many Chinese words share a sound, unlucky associations attach to some numbers and gifts: 四 sì sounds like 死 sǐ death; giving a clock 送钟 sòng zhōng echoes 送终 'attend a funeral'; pears 梨 lí can hint at 离 'separate' among superstitious elders.
Umbrellas 伞 sǎn and green hats for men are also avoided as gifts.

phrases.en: give a clock — sounds like a funeral rite
it's fine (most young people don't mind)

ps: Use softer words around sensitive topics: 没了/走了 for death instead of blunt terms; give fruit baskets, tea or red wine rather than clocks; numbers like 6 (smooth) and 8 (wealth) are auspicious.

phrases.en: may everything go smoothly (6 is lucky)

example.zh: 送礼避免送钟，因为和“送终”同音。
example.py: Sòng lǐ bìmiǎn sòng zhōng, yīnwèi hé “sòngzhōng” tóngyīn.
example.en: Avoid gifting clocks, since it sounds like the funeral phrase.

ps: 8 (八 bā) sounds like 发 fā 'prosper' — phone numbers, floors and wedding dates with 8 are prized. 6 (liù) suggests 溜 'smooth' (六六大顺). 9 (jiǔ) echoes 久 'long-lasting', popular for couples.
Red packets (红包) contain even, lucky sums.
4 (sì) sounds like death, so many buildings skip the 4th, 14th, 24th floors, and 4 is avoided in prices and gifts. Knowing this explains 'missing' buttons in elevators.

phrases.en: sounds like 我爱你 I love you

example.zh: 中国人喜欢 8 和 6，不太喜欢 4。
example.py: Zhōngguó rén xǐhuan bā hé liù, bú tài xǐhuan sì.
example.en: Chinese people favor 8 and 6, and tend to avoid 4.

colors-culture.title: Color Culture · 颜色文化
colors-culture.subtitle: Red for joy, white for both weddings and mourning.

ps: Red (红 hóng) is the color of celebration, luck and the Spring Festival: red envelopes, red lanterns, wedding decorations and the national flag all use it. Red ink for names, however, can imply severing ties — avoid writing names in red.
Gold/yellow signals wealth and imperial history.

White traditionally symbolized mourning (white funeral banners), though modern weddings also use white wedding dresses. Black can be solemn; green hats on a man carry a joke about infidelity — don't gift one.

phrases.en: (idiom) to be cheated on — avoid as a gift

example.zh: 过年贴红色，婚礼也用红色，红色代表好运。
example.py: Guònián tiē hóngsè, hūnlǐ yě yòng hóngsè, hóngsè dàibiǎo hǎoyùn.
example.en: At New Year and weddings red is everywhere — it stands for good fortune.

gifting-culture.title: Gift-Giving · 送礼
gifting-culture.subtitle: What to bring, how to offer, how to receive.

ps: Good guest gifts: fruit, tea, quality snacks, flowers (avoid white chrysanthemums, tied to funerals), or something from your home country. Avoid clocks, pears, umbrellas, sharp objects (they suggest cutting ties), and green hats for men.
Wrap nicely; red and gold wrapping is festive.

phrases.en: a small token of my regard

ps: Offer a gift with both hands and mild words (一点心意). The receiver may politely decline once or twice before accepting — that's 客气, not a real refusal. Receive gifts with both hands and thanks; open later unless invited.

phrases.py: Yì diǎn xiǎo lǐwù, qǐng shōuxià.
phrases.en: A small gift, please accept it.

example.zh: （双手递上）一点家乡的小礼物，请收下。
example.py: （shuāngshǒu dì shàng）Yì diǎn jiāxiāng de xiǎo lǐwù, qǐng shōuxià.
example.en: (Offer with both hands) A small gift from my hometown, please accept it.

idioms.title: Everyday Idioms · 常用成语俗语
idioms.subtitle: Set phrases that make you sound native.

ps: 成语 (chéngyǔ) are compact four-character sayings with old stories behind them. Useful ones: 人山人海 crowds of people; 马马虎虎 so-so; 入乡随俗 when in Rome; 半途而废 give up halfway; 一丝不苟 meticulous.
Use them sparingly and in the right context for maximum charm.

phrases.en: when in Rome, do as Romans do
meticulous, not a thread out of place

ps: Common spoken sayings: 慢慢来 take it easy; 没关系 no problem; 没问题 no problem; 无所谓 whatever/doesn't matter; 加油! keep going!; 没事 it's nothing / I'm fine.

phrases.en: Go for it! / You can do it!

example.zh: 刚来别着急，慢慢来，入乡随俗。
example.py: Gāng lái bié zhāojí, mànmàn lái, rù xiāng suí sú.
example.en: Don't stress as a newcomer — take it easy and follow local ways.
